strengths: The paper tackles a real and well-documented problem in contrastive VLP: hard negative sampling inevitably raises the false-negative rate, and existing fixes rely on fixed thresholds or external pretrained models. The motivation section (Figure 2 quantile/ITM analyses) provides direct empirical evidence for the anchor-specific, time-varying nature of the optimal hardness, which convincingly motivates a learned scheduler rather than a fixed heuristic.

The core idea—parameterizing per-anchor hardness as a quantile q via a lightweight MLP over the sorted similarity distribution matrix, trained with a policy-gradient (REINFORCE) signal from the reduction in MLM loss—is reasonably novel. The authors' claim of being the first learning-based scheduler for the hard-vs-false-negative trade-off appears credible, and the design gracefully reduces to GRIT-VLP when q=1, giving a clean relationship to prior work.

The empirical evaluation is unusually broad: three VLP frameworks (ALBEF, BLIP-2, SigLIP-2), multiple tasks (IRTR, VQA, NLVR2, captioning), both clean (MSCOCO) and web-crawled (CC/SBU, DataComp) settings, wall-clock-time comparisons (0.83C vs 1.0C for ALBEF), learning curves across epochs, and qualitative visualizations of the scheduler's behavior (Figure 5, 6, 9, 10). FALCON achieves the best results in most settings (e.g., Table 1: 62.28 TR R@1 vs 60.96 for MAFA).

Fairness toward baselines is addressed carefully: search space size and thresholds are swept for GRIT-VLP and MAFA (Table 7), DiHT/SRCL are reimplemented, and dynamic scheduling baselines (Progressive-Hardening/Softening) are introduced to isolate the benefit of learned vs. hand-crafted schedules.

The ablations are targeted and informative: they confirm the MLM-loss proxy is superior to contrastive proxies (Table 5 middle, showing L_ITC/L_ITM proxies actively hurt), that instance-level scheduling outperforms batch-level, and that the method is robust to large search spaces where baselines degrade. Limitations (SigLIP-2 asymmetry due to the proxy using only the vision encoder; degraded gains on noisy captions) are honestly discussed.

Reproducibility is good: pseudo-code for both the batch construction and the training loop, hyperparameter tables, dataset statistics, and hardware details are provided; official codebases are used for baselines where available.
weaknesses: The learning signal for the scheduler is a single-sample REINFORCE estimate using the within-step reduction in MLM loss. This is a high-variance, heuristic proxy: maximizing immediate MLM loss reduction may favor batches that are quickly fit rather than those that improve long-term cross-modal alignment, and the paper offers only empirical (ablation-based) support rather than any theoretical or diagnostic analysis of the signal's reliability, variance, or sensitivity to the step size gamma (listed only as 'scheduled' in Table 6, with no schedule given).

The gains over the strongest simple baseline (fixed q=0.5) are modest and inconsistent across metrics/settings—e.g., in Table 1 image retrieval R@5/R@10 the gap is ~1.2 and 0.3 points, and in Table 2 fine-tuned image retrieval MAFA ties FALCON at R@10 90.2. No standard deviations or multi-seed results are reported, so the statistical significance of these margins is unclear.

The method's advantage shrinks precisely in the setting most relevant to the claimed problem: on the noisy 4M web-crawled data (Table 2) and unrefined Conceptual Captions (Table 9 right), gains are small, and the authors attribute this to caption noise hindering the trade-off estimation. This somewhat undercuts the central narrative that FALCON is most valuable when false negatives are prevalent.

The SigLIP-2 experiment reveals a structural limitation: because the generative proxy does not involve the text encoder, text-to-image retrieval gains are marginal (54.15 vs 54.21 R@1). The method's applicability is thus contingent on the existence of a suitable auxiliary objective, limiting generality across contrastive paradigms (e.g., pure CLIP-style setups).

Novelty is incremental relative to GRIT-VLP: the mini-batch construction machinery is inherited, and FALCON mainly generalizes the fixed 'most similar' rule to a learned quantile. Some comparisons are also less apples-to-apples: for SigLIP-2 the training code was unavailable, the loss was modified from sigmoid to softmax, and the SILC/TIPS losses were removed; DiHT and SRCL are author reimplementations.

Presentation issues: Equation (3) conflates notation (expectation vs. single-sample update is unclear), the reward definition Δ uses L_MLM(θ_k) − L_MLM(θ_{k+1}) evaluated on the same batch, which introduces a potential circularity between the VLP model update and the scheduler reward that is not analyzed, and several details (learning-rate schedule for gamma, variance reduction techniques) are deferred or missing.

strengths: The core idea — a learned scheduler for negative hardness in VLP mini-batch construction, trained via a policy-gradient signal from MLM loss reduction — is a genuinely novel framing of the hard-vs-false-negative trade-off, and to the authors' credit it is positioned clearly against GRIT-VLP and MAFA.

The empirical coverage is broad: three distinct VLP frameworks (ALBEF, BLIP-2, SigLIP-2), four downstream tasks (IRTR, VQA, NLVR2, DataComp's 38-task suite), several datasets, wall-clock-time analysis (Fig. 7), and an epoch-wise learning-curve comparison (Fig. 8), which strengthens the evidence base considerably.

The ablations (Table 5) are well targeted: they isolate the search-space size, the choice of proxy objective (MLM vs. contrastive losses), and instance-level vs. batch-level scheduling, and each ablation supports a specific design decision made in the method section.

Baseline fairness is treated seriously: hyperparameter sweeps for GRIT-VLP and MAFA (Table 7), implementation details for methods without code, and honest reporting of cases where FALCON's advantage shrinks (4M-data results in Table 2, noisy-captions results in Table 9 right, SigLIP-2 image retrieval in Table 4).
The method does not require an external pretrained false-negative detector, which is an advantage over MAFA-style filtering and is supported by the DataComp results where MAFA degrades (Table 10).
weaknesses: The central claim — that FALCON adaptively balances hard and false negatives — is never validated directly. False negatives are only identified via a pretrained model for motivation (Fig. 2); the paper never measures the actual false-negative rate in FALCON's constructed batches or shows the scheduler avoids them. The 'balance' is inferred indirectly from the mean-quantile trajectory in Fig. 6, which could equally be explained by a generic difficulty curriculum. This is a material gap between claim and evidence.

The proxy reward (MLM loss reduction between consecutive updates) is a noisy, non-stationary signal trained with REINFORCE-style gradient ascent. The paper provides no analysis of the variance of ∆k, scheduler stability, or sensitivity to the step size γ (reported only as 'scheduled' in Table 6). Given the known brittleness of policy-gradient methods in online settings, this undercuts confidence in reproducibility and robustness.

No results are reported with multiple seeds or confidence intervals anywhere. Several headline gains are small (e.g., BLIP-2 VQA2 val 42.46→42.67, OKVQA 17.94→20.96, SigLIP-2 image retrieval R@1 54.21→54.15, Table 9 noisy setting gains of ~1 point), and without variance estimates the significance of these improvements is unclear.

The scale of evaluation limits the conclusions. The main comparison (Table 1) pretrains on MSCOCO only (~113K images), where many-to-many correspondence — the very phenomenon motivating the method — is comparatively mild. On the 4M web-crawled setting (Table 2), where false negatives should matter most, the gains shrink substantially, and on unrefined web captions (Table 9 right) they are modest. The method's value in the realistic large-scale regime remains only partially demonstrated.

The SigLIP-2 'compatibility' experiment is weakened by non-trivial modifications to the framework (removing SILC/TIPS losses, replacing the sigmoid loss with a softmax loss), so the claimed portability across contrastive paradigms is less clean than presented; the authors do acknowledge the vision-side-only proxy issue, but this amounts to a significant restriction of generality.

The learned scheduler is arguably a heavier mechanism than the problem requires: the result reduces to choosing a scalar quantile q per anchor, and the batch-level ablation (58.78 vs. 61.72 R@1) suggests much of the benefit could potentially be captured by simpler instance-adaptive heuristics that are not compared (e.g., per-anchor similarity-margin thresholds). The related-work section is also relegated entirely to the appendix, omitting engagement with debiased contrastive learning approaches (e.g., Chuang et al. [12]) that address false negatives analytically.
No code release is mentioned, and the online coupling between scheduler updates, queue-based embeddings, and search-space reshuffling adds substantial reproducibility friction.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem in vision-language pretraining: the trade-off between informative hard negatives and harmful false negatives, and the observation that the optimal similarity range is anchor-specific and evolves during training is convincingly supported by Figure 2.

The proposed approach is genuinely novel in framing mini-batch construction as a learning problem: a lightweight scheduler predicts a per-instance hardness quantile, trained via a policy-gradient objective on the reduction in MLM loss. This is a sensible alternative to fixed heuristics and pretrained-model filtering, and the authors correctly show (Table 5, middle) that contrastive-based proxies encourage trivial negatives while the generative proxy does not.

The experimental evidence is unusually thorough for this area: results across three VLP frameworks (ALBEF, BLIP-2, SigLIP-2), multiple downstream tasks (IRTR, VQA, NLVR2, captioning), 4M-dataset zero-shot/fine-tuned retrieval, DataComp evaluation, and a rich set of heuristic baselines (fixed quantiles, progressive hardening/softening, GRIT-VLP, MAFA, DiHT, SRCL).

Baselines appear to be treated fairly: hyperparameters of competing methods (search space size, MAFA threshold) are swept in Appendix 8.1, several baselines outperform original reported numbers, and wall-clock time comparisons (Figure 7) are provided rather than only per-epoch cost.

The ablations directly support the core claims: instance-level scheduling outperforms batch-level scheduling, and the method is robust to large search spaces where baselines degrade (Table 5, Table 7). Honest limitations are acknowledged (e.g., asymmetric gains for SigLIP-2 due to text encoder not participating in the proxy signal; reduced gains on noisy web-crawled captions).
weaknesses: The training signal for the scheduler is a scalar reward (MLM loss reduction) optimized by vanilla policy gradient with no variance reduction or stability analysis. Given that Δ_k is measured from a single gradient update and is inherently noisy, the paper should provide more evidence that the scheduler actually converges to a meaningful policy rather than tracking noise; Figure 6 shows the aggregate trend but no stability/variance analysis across seeds.

The headline comparison (Table 1) is on MSCOCO-only pretraining (~113K images), where many-to-many correspondences are dense and false negatives are most damaging. On the more realistic and larger 4M dataset (Table 2) and on noisy Conceptual Captions (Table 9 right), the margins shrink considerably, which weakens the claim that FALCON substantially outperforms strong baselines in realistic settings.

Some gains are modest and lack statistical significance reporting: e.g., VQA improvements (71.24 vs 71.13 over MAFA) and SigLIP-2 image retrieval where FALCON is slightly worse at R@1 (54.15 vs 54.21). Single-run results without error bars make it hard to judge whether all improvements are reliable.

There is an internal tension: the motivating analysis of false negatives (Figure 2) relies on a pretrained BLIP-129M ITM model, precisely the kind of fixed pretrained-model heuristic the paper criticizes in MAFA. The method itself avoids this reliance, but the evidence base for the motivation inherits these limitations.

The proxy objective conflates generative masked-language prediction with cross-modal contrastive alignment quality; the MLM loss reduction may partially reward easy, visually uninformative batches. The ablation supports MLM over ITC/ITM as a proxy, but a deeper analysis of why this proxy correlates with better embedding quality (beyond downstream accuracy) would strengthen the work.

Added complexity is nontrivial: FALCON costs 0.83C versus GRIT-VLP's 0.65C (a ~28% relative overhead), and the method requires a search-space machinery, quantile subsampling, sorting heuristics, and warm-start epoch; a cleaner justification of each design choice would help reproducibility, though the pseudo-code and hyperparameter tables in the appendix do aid reproduction.
